title: Diophantine approximation spectrum of 4/p by three unit fractions
connection: Schnirelmann-type arguments start from approximate representations. Define δ(p) = min_{x,y,z} |4/p − 1/x − 1/y − 1/z| over x,y,z ≤ p^A (A large enough that all solutions are included); ES(p) ⟺ δ(p) = 0. Study the gap structure of the set of values near 4/p.
why: If near-solutions are abundant at scale p^{−k} and the set of 3-term sums has a 'no isolated gap' property near 4/p, existence might follow by a continuity/pigeonhole step.
first_step: Compute the k smallest nonzero |4/p − Σ| for p ≤ 10⁵ and look for universal patterns in the residual numerators.
refs: Ramare, Ann. Scuola Norm. Sup. Pisa 22 (1995) 645-706

title: Nibble + absorber: random greedy first denominator, absorber for the two-term remainder
connection: Designs exist for all large admissible n via an approximate (nibble) decomposition plus a prepared absorber fixing leftovers. ES: choose x so that m = 4x − p is small and smooth (nibble-like), then 'absorb' via the two-term condition (m/(px) = 1/y + 1/z iff px has divisors a, b with a + b ≡ 0 mod m).
why: Separates ES into a flexible step (many x) and a rigid step (two-term splitting); quantifies how often the absorber succeeds.
first_step: For hard primes, enumerate x near p/4 with m ≤ M and measure the success rate of the two-term step as a function of the smoothness and divisor count of x.

title: Look-ahead greedy: provably terminating 3-term splitting rules
connection: Fibonacci–Sylvester greedy terminates because the numerator decreases; the odd greedy algorithm is open. For 4/p, analyse non-greedy first-step rules (choose x among ⌈p/4⌉ + k for k ≤ K by a look-ahead criterion) and characterise primes where every rule with K ≤ K₀ fails.
why: A finite-look-ahead rule is a bounded procedure (B1 says it must fail for some p under H), but the failure set's structure is informative and computable.
first_step: For each p ≤ 10⁸ compute the least k such that x = ⌈p/4⌉ + k leaves a two-term-solvable remainder; record the distribution and the extreme p.

title: Σ over the first denominator of a two-term representation function (ternary-Goldbach shape)
connection: Ternary Goldbach averages a binary problem over one prime: Σ_p r₂(n − p). ES: R_ES(p) = Σ_x r₂^{EF}((4x − p)/(px)), where r₂^{EF}(m/N) = #{1/y + 1/z = m/N} is a divisor-pair count (a + b ≡ 0 mod m over divisor pairs of N). The average over x is the extra variable that made Goldbach-type problems pointwise.
why: Makes the 'three-variable' structure explicit with a sum over a long free variable x ∈ (p/4, 3p/4), whose length is power-size even if the main term is not.
first_step: Compute for hard p the distribution of r₂^{EF} over x and the correlation between consecutive x; check whether the x-sum behaves like a sum of independent rare events.

title: 8/n exceptions as a built-in falsification test
connection: Kolmogorov/Kahane–Katznelson show almost-everywhere statements can fail on prescribed null sets. ES has a real-world analogue: 8/n fails at 131 and 241 while being 'almost all'. Any ES argument that is uniform in the numerator m without a threshold would prove 8/131 — use this as a mandatory test for every candidate mechanism.
why: Cheap and decisive filter for proof attempts (already in FRONTIER (J)41); worth applying to each upgrade template in this list.
first_step: For each template here (complementary methods, pigeonhole + group law, Hecke relations, …) check whether its ES version would also apply verbatim to 8/131.
refs: Kolmogorov, Fund. Math. 4 (1923)/ C. R. 1926 (everywhere divergent L^1 Fourier series)

title: All-but-finitely-many with genuine small exceptions (Terjanian) — ES-type numerator analogues
connection: Ax–Kochen's statement is true for p > p₀(d) and false for some small p (Terjanian). The ES numerator family behaves similarly: 4/n has no known exception, but 8/n fails at 131, 241. A structural explanation of where p₀(m) lies for m/n would show what makes m = 4 special.
why: Understanding why 4 behaves like 'p₀ = 1' while 8 has small exceptions is a sharp test of any mechanism.
first_step: Tabulate the exceptions of m/n for m ≤ 30 (PW data) and search for a statistic predicting their largest exception (cf. Schinzel's exp(m^{1/3+o(1)})).

title: Basis of order 3 vs order 4: Egyptian 'order' of 4/p is ≤ 4 trivially
connection: Schnirelmann bounds the order of a basis. For unit fractions, 4/p is always a sum of 4 unit fractions (4/p = 1/(k+1) + 3/(p(k+1)), and 3/m splits into ≤ 3 terms); ES asks for order 3. Study the 'order-3 deficiency': which 4-term representations of 4/p are 'one merge away' from a 3-term one (two terms with 1/a + 1/b a unit fraction)?
why: Turns ES into a merging problem on abundant 4-term representations, a different combinatorial entry point.
first_step: For p ≤ 10⁵ enumerate 4-term representations with bounded denominators and count mergeable pairs; compare with the number of 3-term solutions.
refs: Ramare, Ann. Scuola Norm. Sup. Pisa 22 (1995) 645-706

title: Large-degree analogue: ES for m/p as m grows with p
connection: Tao's Sendov proof works for sufficiently high degree, using the degree as a large parameter. ES has a natural large parameter family: m/p for growing m (ES_m). Uniform-in-m results exist for the exceptional set ((D)31: E_m(I) ≪ H exp(−c(log H)^{3/4} m^{−1/4})); study the regime m ≈ log p where Schinzel-type exceptions appear, as a 'large-parameter' analogue.
why: The large-m regime has genuine exceptions; the transition region may show which mechanism protects m = 4.
first_step: Compute the least m(p) for which m/p fails (3-term) for primes p ≤ 10⁵, and the distribution of m(p)/log p.
refs: arXiv:2012.04125 (Tao, Sendov's conjecture for sufficiently high degree polynomials)

title: Croot's 'one target, all colourings' as a pointwise model for ES
connection: Croot's theorem is pointwise in the target (exactly 1) and uniform over colourings — the quantifier structure ES needs (one target 4/p, every p). Study Croot's proof for which step converts averaged Fourier information into a single-target statement.
why: Croot's argument is one of the few in Egyptian fractions where a specific target is hit for every configuration; its key lemma may transfer to 'every p' with a family of targets.
first_step: Read Croot (Ann. Math. 2003) and isolate the single-target step; test whether its numerics (number of terms, smoothness) can be squeezed to 3 terms for targets 4/p.
refs: arXiv:math/0311421 (Croot, On a coloring conjecture about unit fractions, Ann. Math. 157 (2003))

title: Union-closed structure of the family of ES-solvable sets of numerators
connection: Gilmer's method applies to union-closed families. For each n, the set A_n = {m : m/n is a 3-term Egyptian fraction} — is the family {A_n} (or its complements) closed under unions/intersections in a way that forces a frequent element (a numerator m that works for most n)? For m = 4 the conjecture is 'all n'.
why: Odd, but the numerator–denominator incidence structure (with 8/n failing at 131, 241) is a natural set system to analyse with these tools.
first_step: Compute A_n ∩ [1, 30] for n ≤ 10⁵ and test closure properties and element frequencies.
refs: arXiv:2211.09055 (Gilmer, A constant lower bound for the union-closed sets conjecture)

title: Harmonic-sum thresholds for the denominator set of ES solutions
connection: Liu–Sawhney: a set A ⊂ [1, N] with Σ_{n∈A} 1/n ≥ (log N)^{4/5+o(1)} contains S with Σ_{S} 1/n = 1. ES solutions for p use denominators in {multiples of p} ∪ {numbers ≈ p/4 … p²}; compute the 'harmonic mass' of the possible denominator sets and compare with such thresholds (for 3 terms, thresholds are presumably different, but the bookkeeping shows the gap).
why: Quantifies how far ES is from the regime where density-based unit-fraction theorems apply.
first_step: Compute Σ 1/n over the set of denominators appearing in any ES solution for p (data) and over natural supersets.
refs: arXiv:2112.03726 (Bloom, On a density conjecture about unit fractions)

title: Distinct-denominator and ordering refinements as stronger every-n statements
connection: Breusch/Stewart required distinct denominators of a given parity. ES refinements: x < y < z distinct (automatic except special cases), x ≤ p/2, z ≤ p²/2, gcd conditions. Determine the strongest refinement that still holds for all p ≤ 10⁹; it defines the 'tightest' every-p target.
why: The tightest true statement carries the most structure for a proof and the most information for disproof searches.
first_step: Tabulate, for p ≤ 10⁹, the minimal max-denominator over solutions normalised by p², and other extremal statistics.
refs: Breusch, A special case of Egyptian fractions, Amer. Math. Monthly 61 (1954) 200-201

title: FF reciprocity sign (−1)^{deg·deg·(q−1)/2} may resurrect a T1-type square obstruction for q ≡ 3 (mod 4)
connection: T1 (empty certificate lines at odd squares) is a quadratic-reciprocity effect over Q. FF quadratic reciprocity carries a sign depending on degrees and q mod 4, so odd-degree squares in F_3[T], F_7[T] may carry a T1 analogue.
why: If a T1 analogue appears exactly when the reciprocity sign is non-trivial, T1 is pinned to the sign in reciprocity, the 'archimedean' part of Q's reciprocity.
first_step: EXSET_FUNCTION_FIELD Thm 1.3 already shows squares fail U_q for q ≡ 3 (mod 4) — start there. For q = 3, 7 enumerate certificate lines at P = Q² with deg Q odd vs even (deg ≤ 6) and test emptiness; compare FUNCTIONFIELD_ES2 §3 (degree parity).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Two-variable identities for primes represented by a non-principal binary form
connection: Primes p = f(S,T) for a non-principal form f (e.g. disc −23, h = 3) form a non-congruence set. A polynomial identity 4/f(S,T) = Σ 1/X_i(S,T) in Z[S,T] would cover a non-abelian Chebotarev set.
why: It would be a certificate family outside the abelian (congruence) world where Mordell's obstruction lives; the obstruction then concerns which forms represent squares.
first_step: Search ansätze X_i quadratic/quartic in (S,T) for f = 2S²+ST+3T² by solving coefficient equations with a Gröbner basis or LLL.

title: Carlitz cyclotomic fields as the FF analogue of Q(ζ_{4C}) in Type II certificates
connection: Type II certificate conditions over Z are splitting conditions in Q(ζ_{4C}). In FF they become splitting in Carlitz cyclotomic fields K_M, which are abelian with Galois group (F_q[T]/M)^*.
why: Clean class field theory in FF makes the certificate covering problem an explicit set-covering in finite abelian groups; any FF covering bound gives a template for Z.
first_step: Express the FF covering trees of FUNCTIONFIELD_ES as covers of (F_q[T]/M)^* by cosets and compute covering numbers.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES over Z[T]/(T² − D) as Z-module identities = real quadratic world
connection: Identities with denominators in Z[√D] specialize to the real-quadratic world (other_rings Prop 3.3). Viewing them as polynomial identities in T modulo T² − D links the two worlds.
why: Shows whether the real-quadratic universal-divisor identity can be 'traced down' to Z, giving a family over Z of trace-type denominators.
first_step: Take the D = 2 identity of Prop 3.3 and compute Galois traces/norms of its denominators; see if they yield a Z identity with numerator 8 (see trace-descent item).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Function-field Type II ↔ binary quadratic forms over F_q[T] (Artin's imaginary quadratic function fields)
connection: Type II ES data encode representations by binary forms; over F_q[T] with q odd, binary forms have class groups of imaginary quadratic function fields (Artin). Class numbers are given by L-function values (RH known).
why: An FF formula 'ES count at P = combination of class numbers' with RH would give exact asymptotics, whose Z twin is a Dirichlet-class-number formula for ES counts.
first_step: Express the FF Type II count at fixed P as a sum over discriminants of class numbers h(D) and test numerically for q = 3.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Real quadratic O_K with N(ε) = −1: positive ES PROVED via inert ℓ ≡ 3 mod 4 and η ≡ −1 mod ℓ
connection: Prop 3.3: a totally positive unit η with ℓ | 1 + η supplies a universal divisor ℓ ≡ 3 (mod 4). Over Z the only units are ±1, so this step has no direct replacement; its integer shadow is a p-independent divisor of a p-tied integer, which only congruence (B1) supplies.
why: This is the proved twin with the most transparent mechanism; any 'unit-like' integer object (e.g. the Pell/unit-orbit families) is a candidate replacement.
first_step: Read UNIT_ORBIT_ES.md for integer replacements of η and list which ones produce divisors of 4Cp+1 independent of p.

title: Trace descent: Galois-sum an O_K solution to get an integer identity with numerator 8
connection: If 4/n = Σ 1/x_i with x_i ∈ O_K (K real quadratic), adding the conjugate equation gives 8/n = Σ Tr(x_i)/N(x_i). When Tr(x_i) | N(x_i) for each i, this is a 3-term unit-fraction representation of 8/n.
why: Turns the proved real-quadratic world into an integer statement for numerator 8 (Schinzel-type), with an explicit divisibility condition to engineer.
first_step: For the D = 2 identity of Prop 3.3, compute Tr and N of each denominator as polynomials in n and check the divisibility Tr | N on residue classes.

title: Gaussian cone ES (Bradford–Ionascu Conj. 1.1) is OPEN — the Z[i] twin of ES
connection: Denominators in Z[i] with Re, Im of equal sign. The cone is discrete at ∞ and has no small units, so the unit-sum mechanism fails, as over Z. The other_rings principle predicts a genuine lottery problem.
why: A second open twin with richer arithmetic (split primes) — progress there (e.g. density-1 results) could be transported.
first_step: Implement a search for the Gaussian cone ES for Gaussian primes of norm ≤ 10^5 and record failures; check whether failures concentrate at squares as over Z.

title: Eisenstein cone: Z[ω] with denominators in the 60° sector
connection: Z[ω] has 6 units; angular sectors are not closed under multiplication (arguments add), so a positive cone must be a semiring such as N-spans of a few units, or a sector cone with a weaker closure requirement. Each choice gives a different Eisenstein ES.
why: Choosing a closed cone in Z[ω] is itself a non-trivial design question that tests which positivity axioms matter.
first_step: Determine the multiplicatively closed cones in Z[ω] discrete at ∞ (e.g. N-span of {1, −ω²}?) and run the e-slice search in each.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Semiring cone Z_{≥0}[√2]: discrete at one real place, not at the other
connection: C = {a + b√2: a, b ≥ 0} ∖ {0} is multiplicatively closed, ≥ 1 at the identity embedding, but conjugates a − b√2 can be tiny. Intermediate between ℕ (fully discrete) and totally positive O_K (unit-rich).
why: Tests whether discreteness at ONE place suffices for hardness; if ES over this cone is again 'lottery', the archimedean crux is one-place.
first_step: Search the unit-sum mechanism in C: find e ∈ C, e ≡ 3 (mod 4O_K) with e = 1/u + 1/v, u, v ∈ C (note units 1+√2 ∈ C but (1+√2)^{-1} ∉ C).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES over Z[√−d] orders (non-maximal) with Gaussian-style cones
connection: Non-maximal orders (e.g. Z[2i], Z[√−3]) are not integrally closed; unit fractions behave differently at the conductor. ES for rational n in Z[2i] with Re, Im ≥ 0 sits between Z and Z[i].
why: Conductor primes give extra local constraints, a toy model of 'local obstruction at 2' that ES has with numerator 4.
first_step: Compare solution counts for rational p ≤ 10^4 in Z[i] vs Z[2i] cones.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Hurwitz quaternions with positive-definite cone: non-commutative ES
connection: In a definite quaternion order, 1/x = x̄/N(x); require denominators with positive real part or in a cone. Non-commutativity gives more solutions per norm.
why: Quaternion norms connect ES to sums of four squares and Eichler orders; repo QUATERNION_ES treats an equivalent form — the cone version is a separate world.
first_step: Read QUATERNION_ES.md, then test 4/p = Σ 1/x_i with x_i Hurwitz quaternions of positive real part for p ≤ 1000.

title: Imaginary quadratic fields with class number > 1: ES for principal vs non-principal primes
connection: Over O_K with h > 1, a rational prime p ≡ 1 mod 4 may split into non-principal primes; then 4/p has fewer 'divisor' options among principal elements. With a sector cone this is a new hard world.
why: Measures the role of class group in the divisor-in-class lottery; Z has h = 1.
first_step: Take K = Q(√−5), sector cone, test ES for rational p splitting into non-principal primes vs principal ones.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Positive ES over O_K for n ∈ O_K with Galois-conjugate denominators only
connection: Require the three denominators to form a Galois orbit (K cubic, x, σx, σ²x): 4/n = Tr(1/x). Then ES becomes 'n/4 is the reciprocal of a trace of a reciprocal' — a norm-form equation.
why: Gives a cubic norm-form reformulation for rational n: Tr_{K/Q}(1/x) = 4/n; such equations are amenable to Thue/Schmidt or to equidistribution of units.
first_step: For cyclic cubic K of small conductor, solve Tr(1/x) = 4/p for totally positive x ∈ O_K, p ≤ 10^4.

title: p-adic sign patterns: which quadratic-character patterns (χ(x), χ(y), χ(z)) occur among local solutions
connection: Z_p carries no order, but a sign can be a quadratic character. ES over Z_p with denominators in a quadratic-character cone is a local question solvable by Hensel; relevant only as local data.
why: Local data are inputs to Bright–Loughran's no-BM result and the singular series; the cone version records which sign patterns of x, y, z occur locally.
first_step: Compute, for ℓ ≤ 30, which (χ(x), χ(y), χ(z)) sign patterns occur for local solutions of 4/n with n ≡ 1 mod 4 — compare with global solutions' patterns.

title: Global sign patterns of ES solutions vs local predictions (Legendre symbols of x, y, z mod small primes)
connection: For each global solution record (x/ℓ), (y/ℓ), (z/ℓ). If some locally allowed pattern never occurs globally at hard primes, that is a hidden global constraint (reciprocity-type).
why: Hidden global constraints are exactly what T1 is; finding more of them maps the obstruction landscape.
first_step: Using existing solution data for p ≤ 10^6, tabulate patterns at ℓ = 3, 5, 7 and test against local frequencies.

title: Real quadratic fields with N(ε) = +1: other_rings evidence shows coverage, find the proof
connection: For D = 3, 6, 7 (N(ε) = +1) the rational classes were covered numerically. The proof of Prop 3.3 used N(ε) = −1 to get ε^{ℓ+1} ≡ −1; for N(ε) = +1 one needs another route (e.g. ℓ split and ε of even order modulo a prime above ℓ).
why: Completing the classification of real quadratic fields would make 'unit rank ≥ 1 ⇒ ES' a theorem for all real quadratic K.
first_step: For D = 3, find ℓ ≡ 3 mod 4 split in K and a prime 𝔩 | ℓ with ε of even order mod 𝔩 and ε^{j} ≡ −1 mod 𝔩 — then need κ totally positive; test.

title: Eichler orders / quaternion algebras ramified at ∞ and p: ES via ideals of norm p
connection: In the definite quaternion algebra B_{p,∞}, left ideals of norm p correspond to supersingular data; ES-like equations among ideal classes appear in Brandt matrices.
why: Brandt matrices give exact counts of ideal-class relations with Ramanujan bounds; if ES solutions map to Brandt-matrix entries, positivity of counts follows.
first_step: Read bsC_supersingular_transfer.md and check whether any ES count equals a Brandt-matrix entry for small p.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Gaussian cone ES for Gaussian primes vs ES over Z: is there an injection of solutions?
connection: A solution of ES over Z for p is a solution in the Gaussian cone (real denominators are in the cone). Conversely, from a Gaussian-cone solution for rational p, taking norms or real parts may give integer data.
why: If 'Gaussian cone ES for rational p ⇒ integer ES' via a projection, the Gaussian world would be a strengthening to attack.
first_step: Test: for each Gaussian-cone solution of 4/p (p ≤ 1000) check whether real parts or norms yield an integer ES solution.

title: Lipschitz/Hurwitz quaternions with integer coefficients ≥ 0 as cone (semiring N[i,j,k])
connection: The semiring of quaternions with non-negative coefficients is multiplicatively closed? (No: i·i = −1 ∉.) Hence a natural non-commutative cone must be designed (e.g. positive real part + norm conditions).
why: Recording a failed cone design avoids wasted searches and clarifies minimal axioms (multiplicative closure is essential for Lemma 3.1).
first_step: List candidate quaternionic cones and check multiplicative closure; keep only valid ones for a search.

title: ES in rings of integers of CM fields with cone from the maximal real subfield
connection: For a CM field K with totally real K⁺, use denominators in K whose relative norm to K⁺ is totally positive. Units of K⁺ (rank ≥ 1 when [K⁺:Q] ≥ 2) make the unit mechanism available.
why: Another family where infinite units collapse ES; confirms that only Q and imaginary quadratic K (unit rank 0) are hard.
first_step: For Q(ζ_8), test the unit mechanism with units of Q(√2).

title: Imaginary quadratic fields are the only other unit-rank-0 worlds: Bradford–Ionascu cone is the right twin
connection: Number fields with finite unit group are Q and imaginary quadratic fields. So among number fields the ES-hard worlds (with a sensible cone) are exactly Q and imaginary quadratics.
why: Focuses analogue efforts: Gaussian/Eisenstein cone ES are the only number-field twins, and statements proved for them would be closest to Z.
first_step: State as an Assessment in the cone-classification note; list known results for Gaussian cone ES.

title: Quartic residue symbol (A/p)₄ on certificates: hidden finer obstruction?
connection: For p ≡ 1 (4), the quartic symbol refines (A/p). If certificates' quartic symbols are biased (e.g. never i for some class of p), there may be a finer reciprocity structure, as in the Apollonian quartic obstruction.
why: Quartic reciprocity obstructions appeared in HKRS for Apollonian packings. A quartic bias in ES certificates would be a new invariant.
first_step: Note (cheap test): (A/p) = −1 forces A^{(p−1)/4} = ±i, so only the i vs −i split is informative, and it needs a canonical i (e.g. i ≡ a/b mod p from p = a² + b², a odd, b even). With that normalisation, compute the i/−i split over sign-(−1) words, and the ±1 split over sign-(+1) words, for p ≡ 1 (8) < 10⁶.
alt_first_steps: [analogues-0100] For p ≡ 1 mod 8 ≤ 10^6, compute (2/π)₄ (or whether 2 is a quartic residue) and correlate with the type of the smallest ES certificate.

title: Positive ES in Q(√−1) with the cone 'Re > 0 and Im ≥ 0' (half-closed quadrant) vs both-sign cones
connection: Bradford–Ionascu's cone is Re, Im of equal sign; a strict first quadrant is multiplicatively closed only up to 90° sums (it is not closed: i·i). Clarify which quadrant-like sets are closed and which make ES non-trivial.
why: Cone design determines the world; misdesigned cones give trivial or empty problems.
first_step: Check closure of the equal-sign cone (product of two first-quadrant elements can leave the quadrant) — note Bradford–Ionascu's cone may not be multiplicatively closed, and record what they actually require.

title: Odd-denominator ES is impossible (2-adic): the archetype of a constrained-world local obstruction
connection: If x, y, z are odd, xy + yz + zx is odd and xyz odd, so the reduced fraction has odd numerator, while 4/n (n odd) has numerator 4. So no solution. Likewise exactly one even denominator is impossible by 2-adic valuations (the computation confirms).
why: Gives the template for 'congruence-subgroup denominators' worlds: local obstructions are trivial to detect and separate from genuine lottery failures.
first_step: Generalize: for which multiplicative sets H ⊂ (Z/ℓ^k)^* of allowed denominator classes is there a local obstruction? Tabulate for ℓ ≤ 7.
refs: scripts/z52b_analogues_constraints.py (p ≡ 1 mod 4, p < 4000, all solutions enumerated)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Egyptian fractions with restricted prime support (Chen–Elsholtz–Jiang; Czenky–McGovern–Plavnik)
connection: Representations of 1 with denominators in S(p_1,…,p_t) (S-units) are studied; ES in Z[1/S] relates. For ES over ℕ with denominators S-smooth except for factors of p, the count is finite and computable.
why: Gives an explicit finite-world version of ES (bounded prime support) where complete enumeration is possible and failure structure can be studied exactly.
first_step: For S = {2,3,5,7}, enumerate solutions of 4/p = Σ 1/x_i with x_i ∈ p^{0,1}·S-units, p ≤ 10^6; find which p are covered.
alt_first_steps: [free_fable-0116] Compute the smoothness of (x,y,z)/p-part for the first solution of each p ≤ 10⁶; are the non-p parts typically (log p)-smooth? If so, the S-unit equation over a fixed S ∪ {p} is the right finite problem per p.
[signature-0364] Search the literature for restricted-prime-factor unit fraction equations and extract the exact divisor-sum identity.

title: Dessins d'enfants of type (x,y,z) with χ = 4/p − 1: ES certificates as Belyi maps
connection: Finite-index subgroups of Δ(x,y,z) ↔ dessins (bipartite maps) with all white-vertex degrees dividing x, etc. ↔ an ES certificate is the 'type' of a dessin whose Euler-characteristic bookkeeping involves p.
why: Dessins carry a Galois action; if an ES certificate could be read off a canonical dessin attached to p (e.g. from a Belyi map of a curve with p-torsion), existence would be algebraic. Speculative.
first_step: Look for a natural Belyi map attached to p (e.g. on the Fermat curve of exponent p, or X(p)) whose passport (ramification type) gives (x,y,z) with 1/x + 1/y + 1/z = 4/p; X₀(p)-type modular curves have ramification (2,3,∞) — check others.
alt_first_steps: [analogues-0168] Compute fields of moduli of the smallest regular dessins with ES types for p = 5, 13, 17 (via PSL₂ quotients).

title: ES for elements of Z_p (p-adic) with 'positivity' from an embedding into R — not well-defined
connection: Category-error check: Z_p has no archimedean embedding, so positivity cannot be imported; the meaningful p-adic analogues are local solubility (always) and p-adic cones (items in batch B).
why: Record the closed item to avoid repeated consideration.
first_step: None (closed).

title: Gaussian-norm constrained world: failures are NOT explained by mod 8 or the quartic character of 2
connection: Failures of 'all denominators sums of two squares' below 2·10^4 (40 primes) occur in both classes 1 and 5 mod 8, in non-square classes mod 840 (e.g. 709, 829), and 17 of 40 have 2 as a quartic residue (vs 48% overall among p ≡ 1 mod 8). So no simple local/reciprocity explanation is visible.
why: This world therefore looks like a genuine lottery world with fewer tickets than ES — a test bed for the lottery model where failures actually occur, calibrating predicted vs observed failure rates.
first_step: Compute the lottery-model expected number of norm-constrained solutions per p (densities of sums of two squares among Type I/II denominators) and compare predicted with observed failure frequency.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Harmonic numbers' p-adic valuations (Boyd) and the integrality of Σ 1/x
connection: Boyd's conjecture: J_p = {n : p | numerator(H_n)} is finite; studied via p-adic trees. ES at p is a p-adic statement about which unit-fraction sums have valuation −1 at p.
why: p-adic tree methods for harmonic sums might organize ES solutions by p-adic structure (Type I/II = which denominators carry p).
first_step: Low priority; read Boyd's 'A p-adic study of the partial sums of the harmonic series' for tree technique.

title: Cox 'primes of the form x² + ny²': certificate at level d as a ring-class-field splitting condition
connection: A Type I/II certificate at level d is equivalent to p having a specific representation or splitting behaviour in a ring class field of an order in Q(√−d) (QUATERNION_ES / LATTICE_MEETING). Cox's book gives the exact class-field criterion for such representations.
why: It turns 'certificate at level d' into 'Frobenius of p lies in a set S_d of a Galois group'. ES ⇔ p's Frobenius lies in ∪_d S_d, an infinite union of Chebotarev conditions (the B2 shape).
first_step: For d ≤ 10, write S_d explicitly (ring class field of the relevant conductor) and compute the density covered; compare with the Mordell residue-class picture.
alt_first_steps: [analogues-0241] Search for certificate families whose condition is a binary-form representation of p (not a congruence); NONCONG_LIFTS.md may have candidates.
refs: Cox, Primes of the Form x² + ny² (1989)
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Waring-type 'every n is a sum of three triangular numbers' (Gauss) ↔ ES via genus theory
connection: Gauss's Eureka theorem follows from three squares. Problems equivalent to ternary quadratic representability are 'easy'; ES's equation 4xyz = n(xy+yz+zx) is cubic. A quadratic slice (fixing one variable) gives binary problems.
why: Fixing x gives the 2-term problem, whose solvability is a binary-form/divisor question; the union over x is ES. Genus theory over the union is the conceptual gap.
first_step: Context; check whether 'union over x of binary-form problems' has a ternary-form encoding (cf. Borwein–Choi item).

title: The unit mechanism is NOT finite for fixed S: e·κ = 1 + η has infinitely many instances
connection: In e·κ = 1 + η (other_rings Lemma 3.1) only η is an S-unit; e and κ are not, so S-unit-equation finiteness does not apply. E.g. e = 3 divides 1 + 5^{2j+1} for every j. For a fixed S the mechanism therefore offers infinitely many identities, all of the same congruence type.
why: Corrects an over-reach: the reason fixed-S mechanisms cannot prove integer ES is not finiteness but that they are congruence-type (B1) once translated back to Z.
first_step: Record; check whether the infinitely many instances for fixed S ever produce non-congruence integer families (expected: no).

title: Real cyclotomic field Q(ζ_p)^+: cyclotomic units tied to p supply ES solutions; descend by trace
connection: Q(ζ_p)^+ has totally positive cyclotomic units (e.g. squares of (1 − ζ^a)/(1 − ζ) suitably normalized) and p is totally ramified. Positive ES for 4/p holds there by the unit mechanism; tracing a solution down to Q gives 2(p − 1)/p = Σ Tr(1/α_i), an Egyptian-type identity with trace numerators.
why: Provides an explicit p-indexed family of algebraic solutions whose descent might be engineered (choice of unit) to have unit-fraction traces — an algebraic source of p-dependent certificates.
first_step: For p = 5, 13, 17 compute a totally positive cyclotomic unit η ≡ −1 mod an inert-type prime and the resulting solution; compute traces of the denominators.

title: All even with a denominator ≡ 0 mod 8: fails at 13 primes below 8000
connection: The refinement '8/p with a denominator divisible by 4' (i.e. 4/p with all denominators even and one ≡ 0 mod 8) fails at 5, 13, 17, 73, 97, 113, 193, 241, 577, 769, ….
why: Maps the 2-adic fine structure of solutions; combined with the {17, 241} coincidence it suggests a tower of 2-adic strengthenings with growing finite exception sets.
first_step: Build the 2-adic tower: for each (v₂(x), v₂(y), v₂(z)) pattern, list failing primes below 10^4; find patterns with no failures beyond small p.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES over the ring Z[x]/(x² + x + 1) = Z[ω] with cone N[1, −ω²] (semiring spanned by two units)
connection: The N-span of 1 and −ω² (a 60° wedge spanned by two units) is closed under addition; closure under multiplication needs checking ((−ω²)² = ω⁴ = ω, outside the wedge?). Cone design determines whether an Eisenstein twin exists.
why: If no multiplicatively closed discrete cone exists in Z[ω] with full rank, then the Eisenstein world has no faithful ES twin — a structural fact.
first_step: Enumerate small candidate cones generated by units/small elements and test multiplicative closure computationally.

title: Integer statement from the Gaussian twin: ES with denominators of the form a² + b² and a 'sector' constraint
connection: A Gaussian-cone solution for rational p projects (via norms) to an integer equation with denominators that are sums of two squares. The norm-constrained integer world fails at 40 primes below 2·10^4, so any projection must lose this constraint somewhere.
why: Quantifies what the Gaussian world can and cannot give back to Z: norms alone are too restrictive.
first_step: For a few p in the norm-failure list (41, 137), check whether Gaussian-cone solutions exist (if yes, the projection is not via norms).

title: ES for Gaussian n = π with π ≡ 1 mod 4 in Z[i] but denominators in Z (rational): mixed world
connection: Ask for 4/π = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z with x, y, z ∈ Z[i] but two of them rational integers. Mixing rational and Gaussian denominators interpolates between ES and the Gaussian twin.
why: Mixed worlds test whether a single 'extra' algebraic denominator suffices to dissolve difficulty (one complex degree of freedom).
first_step: Brute-force for Gaussian primes of norm ≤ 2000 with two rational denominators.

title: One algebraic denominator: 4/p = 1/x + 1/y + 1/α with α ∈ O_K totally positive, x, y ∈ ℕ
connection: Allowing exactly one denominator from a real quadratic O_K (totally positive) while the others are integers. Then 1/α must be rational, so α is rational unless 1/x + 1/y is irrational — impossible. So this world collapses to ES (or to two algebraic denominators).
why: Shows that algebraic denominators come in conjugate pairs at minimum; the minimal interesting mixed world has 2 algebraic + 1 rational denominator (the trace-norm binary-form item).
first_step: Record; pursue the 2+1 world (batch B 'quadratic orbit ES').

title: Thinned-denominator worlds (norm forms, forbidden primes): failure rates vary hugely with the thinning
connection: (Not what was computed: the census used NORM denominators, which allow primes ≡ 3 mod 4 to even powers.) Norm-thinning results: sums of two squares fail at 40 primes below 2·10^4; Eisenstein norms fail at 451 of 499 below 8000; x² + 2y² norms at 276 of 499. The strict 'no prime factor ≡ 3 mod 4' world is still to be run.
why: The failure rate varies hugely with the thinning set; a quantitative lottery model must predict 40/1125 vs 451/499 vs 276/499 correctly — a sharp test of the model.
first_step: Fit the lottery model's per-p expected count for each thinning (density of allowed denominators ~ C/√log) and compare predicted vs observed failure fractions.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Eisenstein-norm denominators fail for 90% of p: a 3-adic obstruction?
connection: All denominators of the form a² + ab + b² (no prime ≡ 2 mod 3 to an odd power) fails at 451 of 499 primes. Possibly a 3-adic/ cubic-character obstruction like the odd-denominator 2-adic one: norms are ≡ 0, 1 mod 3, and denominators ≡ 1 mod 3 are 3-adically obstructed (batch C).
why: If explained by a local obstruction (sum of three norms ≡ 1 mod 3 forcing a 3-adic contradiction), it's a clean example of the congruence-subgroup obstruction family; otherwise a lottery world.
first_step: Check the 48 surviving primes: do their solutions all involve a denominator divisible by 3? If yes, the obstruction is the 'denominators ≡ 1 mod 3' 3-adic one.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: ES with denominators in a fixed coset of squares: 4/n = Σ 1/(c·s_i²)
connection: Denominators c·s² (c fixed squarefree): 4/(cn)… reduces to 4c'/n = Σ 1/s_i², the square-reciprocal world (batch C). A coset choice c = p makes it p-tied.
why: Square-reciprocal worlds are very sparse; their solvability for specific c might be governed by genus theory, giving a quadratic-forms handle.
first_step: For c ∈ {1, 2, 3, 5, 6} compute which n admit 4/n = Σ 1/(c s_i²) up to 10^5.

title: ES over finite rings Z/p^kZ lifted with Hensel: number of solutions mod p^k as k → ∞ (p-adic density)
connection: The p-adic density of the ES surface at the target prime p (σ_p) controls how Type I/II split solutions. Its exact value (as function of p) enters the singular series and might vanish to higher order at p for structural reasons.
why: A small σ_p would explain why ES counts at p are only polylog; a closed formula is cheap to derive.
first_step: Count solutions of 4xyz ≡ p(xy + yz + zx) (mod p^k) with x, y, z in suitable unit/non-unit patterns for k ≤ 3, small p.

title: ES over the semiring of Pythagorean triples / norm-one elements: Z[i] units of infinite order? none — use Q(i)^×/torsion
connection: Category check: Z[i] has finite units, so a 'norm-one cone' is finite; using Q(i) norm-one elements gives non-integral denominators. Not a meaningful world; recorded as closed.
why: Avoids a dead end.
first_step: None (closed).

title: Gaussian-cone ES for rational p counted by Hecke characters
connection: Solutions in Z[i] with sector constraints correspond to Gaussian integers in angular sectors; counts of Gaussian primes/integers in sectors are given by Hecke Grössencharacters (Kubilius). A sector-count formula for Gaussian-cone ES would use equidistribution of angles.
why: Angular equidistribution is proved (Hecke); if ES's Gaussian twin reduces to 'some solution in a sector', equidistribution of all solutions' angles would prove it for large norm.
first_step: Compute angles of all Z[i] solutions of 4/p (no cone) for p ≤ 1000 and check whether some lies in the cone; test equidistribution.

title: Z[i] without cone: solutions are plentiful; the cone is a 1/4-probability event per solution
connection: If unconstrained Gaussian solutions are many (polylog or more) and angles are equidistributed, the chance that all three denominators land in the cone is ≈ (1/4)³ per solution — so the Gaussian twin is a lottery with known ticket probability.
why: A clean model where the 'lottery' probability is geometric (angles), enabling exact heuristics to compare with the integer lottery.
first_step: Measure the fraction of unconstrained Gaussian solutions with all denominators in the cone for p ≤ 1000.

title: p-adic cone 1 + p^kZ_p: locally OBSTRUCTED, not collapsed
connection: If all denominators lie in 1 + p^kZ_p (k ≥ 1), each 1/x_i is ≡ 1 mod p^k, so the sum is ≡ 3 (mod p^k) and is a p-adic unit; 4/n with p | n has negative valuation. So this cone gives a local obstruction (congruence-subgroup type), not a collapse.
why: Corrects a tempting misapplication of the cone principle: cones of local units impose congruence obstructions; the collapse mechanism needs elements that are small at a sign place.
first_step: Record with the congruence-subgroup obstruction family (batch C items on odd / 1 mod 3 denominators).

title: Adelic interpolation: p-adic solution families at 2 and p glued with archimedean windows
connection: ES at p = existence of a global point; locally at 2, p, ∞ the solution sets are open sets (2-adic patterns, Type I/II at p, size windows at ∞). Strong approximation fails (it's a cubic surface integral-point problem), but measuring the adelic volume of the 'window' gives the expected count.
why: The adelic window volume times the global density should reproduce log²p; mismatch identifies missing local factors.
first_step: Compute the product of local densities at 2, p, ∞ (window) and small primes for the ES integral-point count; compare with Elsholtz–Tao's average.

title: Gaussian numerator ladder: (1+i)^k/π for k = 1..4 interpolates between 2/n (trivial) and 4/n
connection: In Z[i], 4 = −(1+i)⁴, so the Gaussian-cone ES has numerator (1+i)⁴ up to a unit. The intermediate numerators (1+i)² = 2i and (1+i)³ give worlds 'between 2 and 4' that have no integer counterpart.
why: Locating the first k at which the Gaussian-cone problem becomes hard would show whether difficulty is tied to the full dyadic exponent (v_{(1+i)}(4) = 4) or appears earlier — a dyadic resolution invisible over Z.
first_step: Search for Gaussian primes of norm ≤ 2000 whether (1+i)^k/π (k = 1, 2, 3) is a sum of three cone unit fractions; record failures per k.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Dyadic splitting type across imaginary quadratic twins: 2 ramified (Z[i]), inert (Z[ω]), split (Z[(1+√−7)/2])
connection: The numerator 4 factors differently: (1+i)⁴, 2² (inert), (αᾱ)² (split). If ES-type difficulty in cone worlds depends on how 2 splits, the dyadic structure of ES (I3 coordinate 4Z ∪ (8Z − p), m = 8 coincidence) is the integer shadow of that dependence.
why: Gives a controlled experiment on the role of the prime 2 with three otherwise similar worlds.
first_step: Define comparable cones in the three rings (discrete, multiplicatively closed) and compare failure statistics for rational primes p ≤ 2000.

title: Transfer statement E (from the Gaussian twin): ES ⇐ 'Gaussian-cone ES for rational p' + projection
connection: If a projection Z[i]-solutions → Z-solutions existed, the Gaussian twin (with split-prime divisor abundance) would imply ES. The norm-constrained data (40 failures) show norms are not that projection.
why: Identifies a missing map; proving none exists (e.g. by a dimension/degree argument) closes the direction.
first_step: Look for a Galois-equivariant map from Gaussian solutions of 4/p to rational ones (e.g. via real parts of 1/x); test on data.

title: Cone worlds in Z[√2]: compare four cones (ℕ, N[√2], height-positive, totally positive)
connection: A family of four cones in one ring, only partially ordered by inclusion (e.g. √2 ∈ N[√2] is not totally positive), with expected behaviour hard, ?, hard?, easy. Measuring solution counts per cone for rational p gives a direct map of how cone size controls ES.
why: The cleanest single-ring experiment for the cone principle.
first_step: Implement one search with four filters; output solution counts per cone for p ≤ 1000.

title: ES for Hurwitz quaternions of prime norm p: does every p have a quaternion solution with commuting denominators?
connection: Commuting quaternion denominators lie in an imaginary quadratic subfield; so quaternion ES with commuting denominators = union over imaginary quadratic orders inside the quaternion order of cone-ES there.
why: Gives a union-of-imaginary-quadratic-twins world: ES over many Gaussian-like rings at once; existence in at least one might be easy.
first_step: For p ≤ 500, search for quaternion solutions with all denominators in a common Z[√−d] ⊂ Hurwitz order.

title: Profinite world: ES over Ẑ is locally solvable, but a 'sign' via an Ẑ^×-character can obstruct it
connection: Without restrictions ES is solvable in Ẑ (allowing non-unit denominators). Imposing a profinite 'sign' such as χ_{−4}(x_i) = 1 (denominators ≡ 1 mod 4) is obstructed: the reciprocal sum is ≡ 3 (mod 4) while 4/n ≡ 0 (mod 4) 2-adically for odd n. The sterile-point program, by contrast, studies which profinite points avoid all CERTIFICATE classes — not solutions.
why: Clarifies that profinite obstructions to certificates (sterile points, T1) are different from local obstructions to solutions (which ES lacks); character-type 'signs' produce the latter.
first_step: Record; connect to FF_STERILE_* and the T1 statement.

title: Category-error check: 'ES in the field of p-adic numbers with absolute value positivity'
connection: Q_p has no ordering, and |x|_p ≥ 1 is not closed under addition; so 'positive' p-adic ES with |·|_p-positivity is ill-defined beyond cones of units (collapse) — record as closed.
why: Avoids repeated reconsideration.
first_step: None (closed).

title: ES with denominators from a lacunary set (powers times small factors): 4/p = Σ 1/(a_i 2^{k_i})
connection: Denominators of the form small·2^k: 4/p − Σ … requires p | some denominator, so at least one denominator is p·(small)·2^k; the problem becomes a 2-adic digit problem for (stuff)/p — likely solvable only for special p (p | 2^k − small).
why: A lacunary world tied to the multiplicative order of 2 mod p: ES-type solvability ⇔ conditions on ord_p(2), an Artin-type problem.
first_step: For p < 5000, test solvability with denominators a·2^k (a ≤ 15) times p^{0,1}; correlate with ord_p(2).
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Feature: forced object to descend from (fundamental unit, C(2n,n))
connection: Dividing-line feature 'forced object to descend from (fundamental unit, C(2n,n))'. ES LACKS a canonical p-tied object guaranteed to contain a certificate. To supply it one could: candidate forced objects: fundamental unit of Q(√p), the CF period of √p, the class group of Q(√−p), Gauss periods; test whether any yields a certificate
why: Legendre's negative-Pell proof and Bertrand's proof both start from a forced object with exact factorisation.
first_step: For p ≡ 1 mod 24 ≤ 10^6: take ε_p = (t + u√p)/2 and test whether t, u, t±2, etc. contain a divisor ≡ −1 mod 4C for the relevant C.

title: Feature: class-group parametrisation with positivity
connection: Dividing-line feature 'class-group parametrisation with positivity'. ES LACKS (certificates are not known to biject with a class group or genus). To supply it one could: seek a binary/ternary quadratic form Q_p whose representations of a fixed number correspond to ES solutions; then class number > 0 / genus would force existence
why: Three squares, x²+ny² representations: count = class-number-weighted, positivity from Dirichlet's L(1,χ) > 0.
first_step: Write ES Type I solutions as representations by the binary form 4ad·x − f·y patterns; check for a discriminant D(p) attached naturally.

title: Feature: Heegner-type point construction
connection: Dividing-line feature 'Heegner-type point construction'. ES LACKS. To supply it one could: find a modular curve or Shimura curve whose CM points of discriminant related to p map to the ES surface
why: Primes p ≡ 5,7 mod 8 congruent and Sylvester's cube problem are pointwise for every prime in a class via Heegner points.
first_step: Ask whether the ES cubic surface (projective closure) is dominated by a family of curves with modular parametrisations (e.g. via its conic bundle structure).

title: Feature: reciprocity obstruction at a thin set (T1 at odd squares)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'reciprocity obstruction at a thin set (T1 at odd squares)'. ES HAS it, like Apollonian (HKRS), Rickards–Stange, flea orbits, Conjecture H at squares. To supply it one could: exploit it: obstruction theory often comes with a 'reciprocity-corrected' local-global principle that is provable in fat cases (Rickards–Stange)
why: In the proved fat case, knowing exactly the obstruction gives the full answer; ES's analogue would be 'ES fails only for those certificate lines at squares'.
first_step: Compute, for n = m² (m odd), the full set of certificate shapes that survive T1 and check that ES(m²) is always solved by non-line shapes (it is, trivially, since m² composite) — find the prime-level analogue.

title: Feature: Galois-theoretic forcing of divisor classes (cyclotomic/Lucas)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'Galois-theoretic forcing of divisor classes (cyclotomic/Lucas)'. ES LACKS: ES needs divisors ≡ −1 mod 4C of linear forms, which no cyclotomic structure forces. To supply it one could: use Lucas sequences U_n(P,Q) with discriminant D: primitive divisors r of U_n satisfy r ≡ (D/r) mod n, so negative D gives r ≡ −1 mod n for inert r — choose (P,Q) depending on p
why: Zsigmondy/BHV force divisors in classes ±1 mod n; a −1 mod 4C class appears naturally for inert primes.
first_step: Construct for given p a Lucas sequence whose n-th term equals (or divides) 4Cp+1 or a related ES integer; check whether its primitive divisors can be forced inert.

title: Transfer: Type I through binary quadratic forms of discriminant −4d
connection: f | 4a²d + 1 = (2a)²d + 1 means f is primitively represented by a form of discriminant −4d; Type I at (a,d) ⟺ p ≡ −f (mod 4ad) for such f. ES becomes a union of genus/class conditions on p modulo 4ad.
why: Brings class groups and genus theory of Q(√−d) into ES; class-group positivity is a proved-side mechanism.
first_step: For d ≤ 50, compute the set of residues −f mod 4ad realised by represented f, and check how quickly the union over (a,d) covers all classes mod lcm (local covering) vs primes.

title: Transfer: reciprocity across C: simultaneous confinement contradiction
connection: If all prime factors r of N_C lie in H_C ⊂ (ℤ/4C)^× for many C, then quadratic reciprocity links (q/r) for q | C to (N_C/q) = (1/q) = 1. Try to derive a contradiction from many C simultaneously.
why: Exactly how T1 arises at squares; at primes, the reciprocity constraints may be insufficient — finding where they stop is informative.
first_step: Recheck MODP_RECIPROCITY.md and TWISTED_T1.md for the multi-C version.

title: Transfer: Smith's method: ES 'spin' distribution
connection: Koymans–Milovic and Smith control 2-power class group ranks via bilinear 'spin' sums. ES's Type I success for fixed (a,d) is a Jacobi-symbol-type condition on p; the joint distribution over many (a,d) might be a spin system.
why: Smith's method proves 100% results when pointwise criteria lack governing fields — exactly ES's apparent situation.
first_step: Check whether the indicator of 'p solved by (a,d)' can be written via Jacobi symbols (p/q) for q | 4a²d+1 and how they interact for different (a,d).

title: Transfer: Heegner points on modular curves X₀(N) with N tied to p
connection: Look for CM points of discriminant −4p or −p (for p ≡ 1 mod 4 one has Q(√−p)) on a curve mapping to the ES surface.
why: Heegner constructions give O(1)-count pointwise existence at every prime in a class.
first_step: Determine whether the ES surface over Q is rational (it is a cubic surface with rational points, so likely rational) and look for curves of genus ≥ 1 in it parametrised modularly.

title: Transfer: Gaussian-integer lifting of ES
connection: Over ℤ[i], p = ππ̄ splits. Write 4/p = 4/(ππ̄) and look for Gaussian-integer representations that descend to rational ones (norms/traces).
why: Splitting of p ≡ 1 mod 4 is the extra structure available exactly at ES's hard primes.
first_step: Search for identities 4/(ππ̄) = Σ 1/ξ_i with ξ_i ∈ ℤ[i] such that conjugate pairs combine into rational unit fractions.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: Transfer: Class number h(−p) / h(−4p) parity as a lever
connection: For p ≡ 1 mod 4, h(−4p) is even (genus theory); 2-power divisibility depends on representations like p = x² + 32y². Correlate ES certificate shapes with 2-power class group data.
why: Ties ES to Rédei-type structure where governing-field and Smith methods exist.
first_step: Tabulate h(−4p) mod 8 and the minimal ES certificate shape for p ≡ 1 mod 24 ≤ 10^6; look for dependence.

title: Minimal pair: Apollonian (false: reciprocity) vs Zaremba (claimed true)
connection: Apollonian (false: reciprocity) vs Zaremba (claimed true): they differ essentially in one feature — reciprocity obstructions present vs absent (for the standard alphabet). ES's position: ES: reciprocity obstruction present at squares only.
why: Minimal pairs isolate the feature responsible for crossing the dividing line; each is a precise question about ES.
first_step: None.

title: Minimal pair: Artin conjecture (conditional) vs existence of a primitive root (proved)
connection: Artin conjecture (conditional) vs existence of a primitive root (proved): they differ essentially in one feature — fixed base a vs free choice of base. ES's position: ES has free choice of certificate parameters (like free base), which suggests existence should be easier than an Artin-type fixed-witness statement.
why: Minimal pairs isolate the feature responsible for crossing the dividing line; each is a precise question about ES.
first_step: Quantify how much freedom ES has: number of 'independent' parameters vs constraint count.

title: Minimal pair: Ramanujan's form x²+y²+10z² (finite exceptions, GRH) vs x²+y²+z² (proved by genus)
connection: Ramanujan's form x²+y²+10z² (finite exceptions, GRH) vs x²+y²+z² (proved by genus): they differ essentially in one feature — class number of the genus > 1 (spinor genus not a single class). ES's position: ES has no class-number parametrisation at all; closer to the harder member.
why: Minimal pairs isolate the feature responsible for crossing the dividing line; each is a precise question about ES.
first_step: None.

title: Feature: symmetry group of the solution set
connection: Dividing-line feature 'symmetry group of the solution set'. ES HAS only S₃ (permutations) and scaling n ↦ kn. To supply it one could: look for hidden symmetries: Cremona/Geiser involutions of the cubic surface that preserve positivity on some subsets
why: Markoff (Vieta group), Pell (unit group), two squares (involutions) all exploit large symmetry groups.
first_step: Compute birational automorphisms of the ES cubic surface defined over Q (Geiser involutions through rational points) and test whether they map positive integral solutions to integral ones for some pairs.

title: Feature: p-adic / archimedean transition (local densities at ∞)
connection: Dividing-line feature 'p-adic / archimedean transition (local densities at ∞)'. ES positivity region is bounded (finitely many positive solutions). To supply it one could: view the positive solutions as integral points in a compact region of a non-compact surface; volume of region ~ log² p (matches count)
why: Counting in bounded regions with volume → ∞ slowly is the generic 'small count' regime; proofs require effective equidistribution at log scale.
first_step: Compute the volume of the positivity region in Haar/log measure and compare with R(p) on average.

title: Arithmetic statistics of 'ES-failing residue systems' (Cohen–Lenstra style)
connection: Model the subgroups H_C ∌ −1 confining N_C's factors as random subgroups; Cohen–Lenstra-type weights might give the right probabilities for simultaneous confinement.
why: Arithmetic statistics heuristics with correct weights often predict exceptional sets accurately (e.g. Stevenhagen's negative Pell).
first_step: Compute the empirical distribution of the subgroup generated by N_C's prime factors in (ℤ/4C)^× for fixed small C over many p.

title: Stevenhagen-type conjecture for ES: exact density of p solved by families with modulus ≤ M
connection: Stevenhagen predicted the negative-Pell density via a Markov chain on 2-ranks, later proved (Koymans–Pagano). For ES, a Markov-chain model over growing family sets could predict exact densities at finite M.
why: Exact finite-M densities are provable (Chebotarev); comparing them with a model checks the model's dependence structure.
first_step: Compute exact densities of primes solved by families with 4ad ≤ M for M ≤ 200 (finite CRT computation) and fit decay of the unsolved density.
alt_first_steps: [upgrades-0163] Compute empirical densities of failing-at-all-C ≤ K for K = 1..20 and compare with the independence model and with a Rédei-type model.

title: Connection: Type I families carry a quadratic-character condition: Type I at (a,d) needs (d/p) = −1
connection: Elementary: every prime r | f | (2a)²d + 1 has (−d/r) = 1, so the Kronecker character χ = (−4d/·) has χ(f) = 1; p ≡ −f (mod 4d) then gives (−4d/p) = χ(−1) = −1, i.e. (d/p) = −1 for p ≡ 1 mod 4. Hence a Type I solution at (a,d) exists only if d is a non-residue pattern for p, so the least Type I parameter has d ≥ n(p)-type size, and Type I is dead at squares (T1 for Type I).
why: Explains the correlation result (families sharing d share the character condition) and the n(p) trend in one line. Almost certainly the campaign's 'sign layer' (F6) in different notation.
first_step: Check the analogous condition for Type II (e | a+b, 4ab | p+e) and confirm against T1_TEMPLATE.md; then re-run the correlation test within fixed-d groups.

title: a_p(32a1) mod 8 is just (2/p)
connection: The strong correlation of U(p) with a_p(y²=x³−x) mod 8 (ρ=+0.55) is identical to that with (2/p) (ρ=−0.55): for this CM curve a_p mod 8 encodes p mod 8.

title: Least primitive root vs U: ρ = −0.57 (proxy check)
connection: The least primitive root g(p) is a QNR, so g(p) ≥ least QNR; its correlation is weaker than least QNR (−0.66).
why: Proxy relationship; recorded to avoid double-counting in multi-feature models.

title: Real quadratic regulator log ε_p anticorrelates with U(p) (ρ = −0.44)
connection: log ε_p and log ε_p/√p correlate −0.44 / −0.51 with U(p)-residual; h(p) alone ≈ 0 (−0.04); CF period of √p −0.27.
why: By the class number formula, 2h(p)R/√p = L(1,χ_p) (R = log ε_p): the regulator carries the L-value since h(p)=1 mostly; a direct ES ↔ fundamental unit link is the CF/Pell side of the CF-length forms of ES (ES₅).
first_step: Correlate the five-slice / λ(p) ≤ 3 certificate counts with the CF period of √p and with the regulator.

title: h(−3p) correlates positively with U(p) (ρ=+0.46)
connection: U(p) residual vs h(−3p) (imaginary quadratic field Q(√−3p)) ρ = +0.46; vs h(−4p) only +0.08 (raw) / +0.14 (normalised).
why: χ_{−3p}(q) = (−3/q)(p/q): another twist; ES identities with denominator 3 (p ≡ 2 mod 3 classes) suggest the −3 twist is natural.
first_step: Fit log U on all of log L(1,χ_{dp}) for d ∈ {1,−1,−3,−4,−8,5,−20,…} jointly and identify the minimal set.

title: '4-divisible ES': 16/p last failure ≤ 10⁵ is 83449 — an R-zero
connection: 16/p failures (38 primes ≤ 10⁵) include 193, 577, 1201, 2521, 3361, 3169, 4801, 33601, 36529, 78721 and end at 83449, which is also a (★) failure.
why: Two independent hardness tests pick out the same large prime 83449: suggests a shared 2-adic obstruction (p ≡ 1 mod 16? 83449 mod 16 = 9) worth isolating.
first_step: Compute v₂(p−1), p mod 16/32/64 for all 16/p failures and for the 14 R-zeros; test whether 2-adic depth predicts both.
areas: ES variants, function fields & other rings

title: U₈(p) = number of all-even ES solutions of 4/p
connection: By scaling, U₈(p) counts solutions of 4/p with x, y, z even; at primes: 0,0,1,3,0,3,0,2,7,4,12,6,…
why: Ratio U₈(p)/U₄(p) is the 'even fraction' of ES solutions — a 2-adic statistic; if it tends to a constant, even-ES is ES with a constant-factor loss.
first_step: Compute U₈(p)/U₄(p) average by p mod 8 and mod 16; compare with the 2-adic local density of the ES surface.

title: 8/n failures 131 and 241 vs ES hardness of 131 (≡ 3 mod 4) and 241
connection: 241 is a top-30 hard prime for 4/p and the last 8/p failure; 131 ≡ 3 (mod 4) is easy for 4/p.
why: Mixed picture: the even-ES failures are not explained by 4/p hardness alone; 131 needs a separate 2-adic explanation.
first_step: Examine all ES solutions of 4/131 and why none has all-even denominators (parity of x,y,z patterns).

title: Composite R-zeros include the pseudosquare 2641 = 19·139
connection: Composite non-square n ≡ 1 (4) with R(n) = 0: 57, 105, 177, 249, 345, 465, 777, 801, 969, 1345, 1465, 1617, …, 2641, …; 2641 is Lehmer's pseudosquare L₁₃ (A002189) and also an x=(n+3)/4 greedy failure.
why: Pseudosquares mimic squares for all small-prime Legendre symbols; T1 kills squares, so pseudosquares should be near-T1 — a quantitative 'approximate reciprocity obstruction'.
first_step: Compute R, U, Uv, I3 at all pseudosquares A002189 up to 10¹⁰ (targeted divisor-form computation) and compare with typical values.

title: Higher-power residue characters of 2,3,5,7 have no detectable effect on ES counts
connection: Within strata of fixed quadratic profile ((2/p),(3/p),(5/p),(7/p)), whether a ∈ {2,3,5,7} is a cubic/quartic/octic residue mod p shifts mean residual log U(p), k₁, k₂, R(p) by |Δ| ≤ 0.03 (largest −0.029; the attached Mann–Whitney p-values are unstratified tests, smallest 0.015 among 48 tests — consistent with null after multiple testing).
why: Data counterpart of the genus/higher-character split (FRONTIER §2.1): order ≥ 3 characters at small primes don't bias counts; all systematic arithmetic dependence is quadratic (plus p−1 structure).
first_step: Repeat with characters of order 3,4 of larger moduli (q ≤ 50) and with the full X(n) decomposition on (★).

title: 2-adic depth matters: p ≡ 1 (16) has 9% fewer ES solutions than p ≡ 9 (16)
connection: Among p ≡ 1 (8), residual log U(p) is lower by 0.094 when p ≡ 1 (16) (k₁ −0.098, k₂ −0.080, R −0.051); next level 32 vs 16 only −0.013; 9 vs 3: −0.030; 25 vs 5: −0.021.
why: Not explained by quadratic characters ((2/p) = 1 in both classes) nor by the quartic character of 2 (null): it is the multiplicative depth of p−1 at 2 — local densities of the ES surface at 2 depend on p mod 16.
first_step: Compute the 2-adic local density of {4/p = 1/x+1/y+1/z} as a function of p mod 2^k and compare to the observed 9% gap.

title: Quartic residuosity of 2 (p = x² + 64y²) is irrelevant for ES counts
connection: Among p ≡ 1 (8), '2 is a 4th power mod p' shifts residual log U by +0.008 (MW p = 0.10).
why: Rules out a tempting Gauss-type link (p = x²+64y²) to hardness; the Neumann–Setzer form p = u²+64 is a different condition (see next item).
first_step: None needed; record as negative fingerprint.

title: Real class number h(p) is uncorrelated with U(p) (−0.04)
connection: Since h(p) = 1 for most p ≡ 1 (4) at this size, only the regulator carries the L-value; h(p) alone is uninformative.
why: Negative fingerprint: avoids chasing 'class group of Q(√p)' explanations.
first_step: None.

title: r₃(p) = 12 h(−4p) for p ≡ 1 (4): ES counts vs sums of three squares
connection: By Gauss, r₃(p) = 12h(−4p) at p ≡ 1 (mod 4); so U's weak correlation with h(−4p) (+0.08 raw, +0.14 normalised) is also its correlation with r₃(p).
why: THREE_SQUARES.md explored ES ↔ ternary forms; data say the three-squares count is only a weak predictor — the right ternary form, if any, is not x²+y²+z².
first_step: Correlate U(p) with representation numbers of other ternary forms of small discriminant (genus theory via Hurwitz numbers H(4p), H(8p), H(3p)).

title: Which ternary quadratic form's r_Q(p) best predicts U(p)?
connection: Compute-and-check: for all reduced positive ternary forms Q of discriminant ≤ 200, compute r_Q(p) at p ≡ 1 (4) ≤ 10⁵ and the Spearman with U(p) residual.
why: If some Q stands out, ES counts might be (asymptotically) a theta coefficient — the Kudla/Siegel–Weil route (KUDLA_ES.md).
first_step: Use pari qfrep on the Brandt–Intrau list (discriminant ≤ 200) and rank by correlation.

title: Hurwitz class numbers H(4p), H(8p), H(3p) jointly vs ES counts
connection: Hurwitz numbers are coefficients of weight-3/2 Eisenstein series; a linear combination of H(dp)/√p could match the χ-twist dependence found for k₁/k₂.
why: Would give a modular-form 'shadow' of the ES main term, testable to high precision.
first_step: Fit log k₂ on log H(4p)/√p, log H(8p)/√p, log H(3p)/√p; inspect coefficients for rational structure.

title: Sum of two squares p = a² + b² and the Hecke-angle of p vs ES-hardness
connection: Primes p ≡ 1 (4) have a Gaussian angle θ_p (p = a² + b²). Hecke Grössencharacters equidistribute θ_p. If ES-hardness (e.g. large least certificate level, or λ(p) large) correlated with θ_p, ES would interact with ℤ[i]-arithmetic.
why: It is cheap and tests whether the Gaussian structure that p ≡ 1 (4) brings carries ES information. A null result rules out a class of approaches.
first_step: For p < 10⁸, correlate min certificate level / λ(p) / N₋(p) with θ_p and with a mod small numbers.
alt_first_steps: [fingerprint-0127] Also test cos(4θ_p), cos(8θ_p) for the Hecke characters of Q(i) (Kubilius) — expect null.

title: ord_p(2)/(p−1) correlates +0.45 with U(p)
connection: Higher multiplicative order of 2 mod p ⇒ more solutions; partly via (2/p) (2 is a QNR ⇒ index odd…), partly via p−1 smoothness.
why: Artin-type data (order of 2) is a cheap proxy that might enter ES via 2-power denominators (TWO_POWER_LADDER.md).
first_step: Partial correlation controlling for (2/p) and τ(p−1); compare with ord_p(3), ord_p(5).

title: Type-A failures: 193 has h(−4p) in the bottom 2%, 2521 and 66529 have L(1,χ_p) at the 95th percentile
connection: 193: least QNR 5, h(−4p) quantile 0.019, L(1,χ_p) quantile 0.56; 2521: least QNR 11, L quantile 0.95; 66529: least QNR 13, L quantile 0.95.
why: Type A hardness looks χ_p-driven at 2521, 66529 but 193 is a χ_{−4p} (small class number) case — the two mechanisms both occur among the three Type-A failures.
first_step: Compute both quantiles for all Type-A near-failures (primes where the b=1 line has exactly 1–2 certificates) ≤ 10⁸.

title: ES hardness vs Wieferich-type / Fermat-quotient data
connection: Compute-and-check: correlation of U(p) with q_p(2) = (2^{p−1} − 1)/p mod p (Fermat quotient) — a p-adic invariant of 2.
why: Would test whether p-adic (mod p²) information about small primes affects ES; expected null, but cheap and a clean negative.
first_step: Compute q_p(2) mod p for p ≤ 2·10⁵, normalise to [0,1), Spearman with residual U.

title: Primes p with p−1 = 2^k·m, m small: Fermat-like primes as hard cases
connection: Fermat primes 17, 257, 65537 have p ≡ 1 mod 2⁴, 2⁸, 2¹⁶ respectively; compute U(p)/log²p for them: the 2-adic depth effect (−9% per level?) would compound.
why: Direct test of whether 2-adic depth effect saturates (32 vs 16 effect was small) or compounds.
first_step: Run z52b_count on 65537, 257, 17 and on primes 2^k·3+1, 2^k·5+1.

title: ES hardness index vs class number of Q(ζ_p)^+? (too expensive; proxy via h(p))
connection: Compute-and-check (proxy): cyclotomic class-number data are unavailable at scale; the quadratic subfield Q(√p) (h(p) null) is the only cheap proxy.
why: Records that the cyclotomic-unit / Vandiver-type world shows no signal at the quadratic level.
first_step: Skip unless a specific cyclotomic mechanism is proposed.

title: Proth primes are not hard: 65537 (ratio 0.96), 786433 (0.92), 5767169 (1.44), 104857601 (1.62)
connection: Deep 2-adic structure alone (p ≡ 1 mod 2^k) does not make ES hard; 193 = 3·2⁶+1 (0.22), 97 (0.38), 769 (0.41) moderately hard at small size.
why: Separates 2-adic depth from the full smooth-p−1 profile; ES hardness needs many small primes simultaneously ≡ 1-ish, not one deep prime power.
first_step: Regress U(p)/log² on v₂(p−1), v₃(p−1), v₅(p−1) jointly with the χ_p Euler product to apportion.

title: 2-adic depth effect saturates at 16
why: The 2-adic local density of ES solutions seems to depend on p mod 16 only — a finite local datum, consistent with the 'four-adic input' picture (FOUR_ADIC_INPUT.md).
first_step: Compute the exact 2-adic density of the ES surface at p mod 64 by counting solutions mod 2^k.

title: 241 = 240 + 1 as a universal small outlier
connection: 241 appears in: 8/p failures (last), 16/p and 20/p failures (not 12/p), '4 | some denominator' failures (last), 'no 3' failures (unique), U-hard top 30, greedy x = (p+3)/4 failures, z ≤ p^{1.75} failures (first).
why: p − 1 = 240 = 2⁴·3·5 — 241 ≡ 1 (mod 16, 3, 5) is the smallest prime with simultaneous deep 2-adic and 3,5 structure; a natural test case for every new certificate family.
first_step: Add 241, 2521, 193 to every new family's unit tests; record which families certify them.

title: Rédei 4-/8-rank of Cl(−4p) has no effect (h(−4p) mod 16 strata differ by ≤ 0.016 in residual log counts)
connection: For p ≡ 1 (8), residual log U, k₁, k₂, R by h(−4p) mod 16 ∈ {0,4,8,12}: |differences| ≤ 0.016.
why: Another higher-character null: 8-rank (Barrucand–Cohn: p = x²+32y²) governs quartic/octic symbols, which the data already showed are irrelevant.
first_step: None; record.

title: Markov primes vs 12/p failures: {2, 5, 13, 29, 433} = Markov ∩ fail(12) ≤ 10⁵
connection: Markov primes ≤ 10⁵: 2,5,13,29,89,233,433,1597,2897,5741,7561,28657,33461,43261,96557; five lie in the 22-element 12/p failure set (and the same five in fail(24)); 433 is the notable one.
why: Probably small-number coincidence, but Markov numbers m have −1 and other small quantities as QRs mod m (m | a²+b² with structured a, b) — a quadratic-residue profile like ES-hard primes; MARKOFF_ES.md explores Markov ↔ ES.
first_step: Compute the least QNR / L(1,χ_m) quantile for Markov primes and test enrichment in all m/p failure sets with a permutation test.
